tagline.text: A museum in the old home of Father Burgos, one of the three Gomburza priests

location.label: Location
location.text: Burgos Street, Vigan City, Ilocos Sur (a few minutes' walk from Plaza Salcedo)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱0–200 (free entry or a small donation; transport extra)

children.text: This ancestral house in Vigan was built in 1788 and is part of the National Museum’s Ilocos complex. It introduces Father José Burgos and historical life in Ilocos. The nearby Old Carcel Museum displays the Basi Revolt paintings.

Padre Burgos House is an old mansion on Burgos Street in Vigan City, Ilocos Sur. According to Wikipedia it was built in 1788, and it is remembered as the home of José Burgos (1837–1872), a Filipino Catholic priest and reformer. Today it is a museum run by the National Museum of the Philippines under the name Padre Burgos Museum. It is within walking distance of the busy Calle Crisologo and not far from Plaza Salcedo, the central square, so it fits easily into a one-day Vigan itinerary.

The house matters because the building and the man behind it tell one story together. José Burgos was a leading figure in the secularization movement, which argued that Filipino priests deserved the same standing as Spanish friars. After the Cavite Mutiny of January 1872, the Spanish authorities arrested him on charges of sedition together with the priests Mariano Gómez and Jacinto Zamora. On February 17, 1872, the three were executed by garrote at Bagumbayan, today's Rizal Park in Manila. The three priests are collectively known as Gomburza. The event is said to have deeply affected José Rizal and to have inspired him to write his novel El Filibusterismo.

The architecture is worth a look too. The house is an early example of the bahay na bato (a traditional Philippine house of stone and timber) and is smaller and sits lower to the ground than the larger Vigan mansions built later. The ground floor has stone walls and was used for storage, while the upper floor has a wooden frame and was the living space. Behind the large wooden front door, a carriageway (zaguan) leads to a grand wooden staircase, which is the signature view of the house. The plain exterior makes it easier to imagine everyday life in the old days.

The museum opened in 1975 as the Ayala Museum–Vigan, run by the Filipinas Foundation of the Ayala group. It was donated to the Ilocos Historical and Cultural Foundation in 1987 and passed to the National Museum in 1989. In 2015 the National Museum Ilocos network was inaugurated. The house forms the Ilocos regional museum complex together with its neighbor, the old provincial jail known as the Old Carcel, and the Magsingal Museum. This guide is for travelers staying a day or two in Vigan who are interested in history and architecture. Opening hours and admission rules can change, so check the latest announcements before you go.

According to Wikipedia, the house was built in 1788. It is listed among the Philippines' National Cultural Treasures together with the Mestizo District and the Leona Florentino House. Walking through the old town, you will spot the low stone walls and wooden upper floor right away.

The ground floor is built of stone and was used for storage, while the upper floor has a wooden frame and was used for living. This style developed in the Philippines, where earthquakes and typhoons are common. Compared with the larger mansions built later in Vigan, this house is smaller and lower, showing what an early bahay na bato looked like.

Past the large wooden door is a carriageway (zaguan) where carriages once passed, and behind it a large wooden staircase rises to the upper floor. Look at the banister and the grain of the wooden floor. Follow the on-site rules for photography.

blocks.title: A copy of Noli Me Tángere

children.text: The museum is said to hold one of the original copies of José Rizal's novel Noli Me Tángere. Depending on how it is displayed, you may see the book behind glass, so check the current exhibit on site.
The 14 oil paintings of the 1807 revolt against the sugarcane wine monopoly are in the
south wing of the nearby Old Carcel Museum
. Both buildings are part of the National Museum’s Ilocos complex.

Burgos, who is said to have been born in Vigan in 1837, was a scholar-priest who studied at the University of Santo Tomas. In this house you can read about his execution in 1872 and the reform movement. It lets you see Vigan's history not just as sightseeing but as connected to the roots of the Philippine independence movement.

The National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP) installed a historical marker on the front of the building in 1939. The marker tells visitors that the house is connected with Burgos. A photo of the façade with the marker and signboard makes a good souvenir of your visit.

blocks.title: Part of the Ilocos museum complex

children.text: The house belongs to the National Museum's Ilocos regional museum complex, together with the old jail known as the Old Carcel and the Magsingal Museum. You can combine several museums and squares in Vigan on foot in one day, so this house works well as the center of a history-themed route.

items.title: Half-day Vigan history walk
items.subtitle: From the museum to the plaza and Calle Crisologo

children.text: Arrive at Padre Burgos House when it opens. Its opening hours are known to be
on Wikivoyage, but another guide lists Tuesday–Sunday 09:30–17:00 (last entry 16:30, closed Mondays), so sources differ; confirm before you go.
See the wooden staircase and period furnishings at the Burgos House, then go to the nearby Old Carcel Museum for the Basi Revolt paintings.
Walk to Plaza Salcedo and look around the central obelisk and Vigan Cathedral.
Have an early lunch of Vigan empanada or sinanglao at a restaurant near the cathedral.
Stroll the cobblestones of Calle Crisologo and take a kalesa (horse-drawn carriage) ride.
End the day at Plaza Salcedo in time for the dancing fountain in the evening.
The museum is small, and
1–2 hours
is enough even if you take your time. Spend the rest of the day walking and eating.
Walk to the nearby museums, starting with Padre Burgos House.
Walk around Vigan Cathedral, Plaza Burgos and Calle Crisologo, and take a kalesa ride.
Take a tricycle to the Bantay Church and bell tower area.
If you have time, head north to Sinait Church or Paoay Church.
Buses run on fixed schedules, so if you are returning to Manila, check the timetable in advance.
Vigan is about 400 km from Manila, and the trip takes about
7–10 hours
by bus or car. Companies such as Partas, Dominion Bus Lines, Viron Transit and St. Joseph (Aniceto Transit) depart from Quezon City and other points in Metro Manila.

The Partas fare page (2026) lists Manila–Vigan at ₱600 regular, ₱700 deluxe, ₱850 super deluxe and ₱1,000 luxury, while another booking site gives about ₱836–886 for deluxe, so fares vary by company, class and season. Wikivoyage's Dominion fare of ₱580 dates from 2017 and is out of date. Check the current fare when you book.
Many buses run overnight. If you aim for an early-morning arrival, you can use a whole day in Vigan.
As of September 2023, Vigan's own airport reportedly had no scheduled flights. The nearest airport is Laoag International Airport (LAO), about
1 hour 30 minutes
away by car.
Flights between Manila and Laoag are reported to operate daily. Check the schedule with the airline, and travel from Laoag to Vigan by bus, van or rental car.
A 2025 travel blog puts basic tricycle fares within the city at about
(Wikivoyage's ₱8–10 is an old figure); it varies with distance and passengers, so confirm the fare before you ride.
A 2025 blog puts a kalesa (horse-drawn carriage) at about
per hour (some guides quote more, around ₱250), or Wikivoyage's about
for a full day of 6–7 hours. Agree on the route and fare with the driver first.
The center of the old town is best explored on foot.
Vigan has a tropical savanna climate, with a dry season from about November to April and a wet season from May to October. The average temperature is about
. The museum is indoors and can be visited in the rain, but kalesa rides and walking are more comfortable in the dry season.

Wikipedia says Vigan is affected by roughly 7 to 10 typhoons a year (not an official count; travel guides likewise note occasional typhoons in the rainy season), so it is safer to check the forecast if you visit from August to October. Christmas, New Year and the Ilocos Sur Festival in January are crowded, so book accommodation early.

Vigan has many boutique hotels and restored old houses in the historic district. Wikivoyage lists Vigan Hotel at about ₱500 for a double, Casa Teofila Lodge at about ₱1,079–1,476, Villa Angela Heritage House at about ₱1,500–2,800 and El Juliana Hotel at about ₱1,500. Prices rise and fall with the season, so check when you book. A place in the old town within walking distance of Padre Burgos House is the most convenient.

Typical food includes Vigan empanada (a fried rice-flour shell filled with vegetables, egg and sausage), sinanglao (a breakfast beef noodle soup), arroz caldo, miki and okoy. Wikivoyage lists Insiang's Empanada (
) and First Sinanglaoan (
). Vigan longganisa is said to be spicy, unlike the sweeter Pampanga version.
The museum is known to be open
on Wikivoyage, but another guide lists Tuesday–Sunday 09:30–17:00 and closed Mondays, so check with the National Museum Ilocos (nmviganilocos@gmail.com) or the latest announcements before you go.
Entry is described as free, but this may change, so confirm on site.
After the July 2022 earthquake, some of Vigan's heritage sites were under repair. Parts of this house may also be closed off.
Go in the morning when it is quiet and you can look around in peace.
The wooden stairs and floors are old, so leave large bags behind and walk carefully.
It is close to Plaza Salcedo, so combine the square, the cathedral and Calle Crisologo in one walking route.
Repair work after the 2022 earthquake may mean some areas are closed. Check the current access before you visit.
Opening hours and admission rules can change often, so the times in this guide are only a reference based on Wikivoyage.
The museum is an old wooden building, so do not run or lean on the railings.
Agree on the fare and route before you board a kalesa or tricycle, and carry small bills.
During typhoon season (August–October), transport plans can change, so leave some slack.
Follow the on-site rules on photography in the exhibits.

Vigan
. Calle Crisologo, the cathedral and Plaza Salcedo are all within walking distance.

This central square has a 17th-century obelisk and a dancing fountain, and is also known as the place where Gabriela Silang was executed by the Spanish authorities in September 1763. It is a few minutes' walk away.
